text:
Filling it isn't free, either. You pay for every input token, every turn. A five hundred thousand token document, over ten turns, is five million tokens billed, unless a cache steps in. And the model doesn't read it all equally well. Facts at the start and the end come back reliably. The middle sags. It's called lost in the middle. So a bigger window is permission, not a recommendation.

Why did long context take years to build? Every token attends to every other token, so the work grows with the square of the length. From eight thousand tokens to a million is a hundred and twenty-five times the text... and over fifteen thousand times the work. Reasoning models spend tokens on purpose.

A reasoning model writes out its working before it answers: attempts, checks, corrections. Those are thinking tokens. It's the same next-token machine, with nothing new inside. What changed is the training. It's rewarded for answers that can be checked, like math with a known result, or code that passes its tests. So habits like checking its own work get reinforced. Here it tries simple interest, catches the slip, and redoes it as compound growth.

More thinking helps, up to a point. The first five hundred tokens buy nearly two thirds of the gain. Past eight thousand, doubling the budget buys nothing at all. It pays off where steps can be checked, like math, code and planning. But no amount of thinking recalls a fact it never had. And on an easy problem, more thinking can even talk it out of a right first answer.

And thinking tokens are output tokens, billed whether you see them or not. In that answer, you'd read thirteen tokens and pay output prices for a hundred and nineteen. So set the lowest effort that passes your own tests, on purpose. Every token the model reads, writes or thinks ends up on the bill. So what does a token actually cost?
